Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the RetailWave Q4 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question and answer session. Instructions for joining the question and answer session will be given at that time. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to RetailWave's Q4 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Alex Rivera, CEO; Jordan Lee, CFO; and Taylor Kim, COO.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call may contain forward-looking statements, including our expectations for future financial performance, business strategies, and market trends. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete list of these risks and uncertainties.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, CEO of RetailWave.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good afternoon, everyone. We are pleased to report a strong Q4 performance, driven by the effectiveness of our marketing campaigns in boosting brand awareness and customer acquisition, alongside the early success of our new product launches. Our focus remains on optimizing the impact of promotional activities to drive sales while protecting profitability. We are also excited about the initial traction we are seeing with our AI-driven personalization engine, which we believe will significantly enhance conversion rates and customer lifetime value. Finally, we are committed to expanding our take rate through disciplined pricing and mix shifts.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Jordan, our CFO, to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Jordan Lee:
Thank you, Alex. Our Q4 revenue was $2.1 billion, an increase of 25% year-over-year. Gross margin was 42%, driven by a favorable mix toward high-margin private-label products and supply chain efficiencies from our optimized fulfillment network. Operating expenses were $850 million, representing 40% of revenue, reflecting disciplined investments in technology and marketing scaled with our growth.

Our net income for the quarter was $250 million, or $1.20 per share. We ended the quarter with $1.5 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are reaffirming our full-year guidance of revenue between $8.5 billion and $9.0 billion, with adjusted EBITDA margins of 12-14%.

Thank you, Alex. I'll now dive into the effectiveness of our marketing campaigns, with a focus on brand awareness and customer acquisition—two pillars that have driven our Q4 results and positioned RetailWave for accelerated growth in FY25. As a leading omnichannel e-commerce player in fashion, beauty, and consumer electronics, we've leaned heavily into data-driven, AI-optimized strategies to navigate a competitive landscape marked by rising ad costs, privacy changes like iOS 14.5+, and the shift toward social commerce. Let me break this down with the key metrics, channel performance, regional insights, and our strategic playbook.

First, brand awareness. We saw a robust 28% year-over-year lift in aided brand recall among our target 18-34 demographic, per our quarterly Nielsen survey of 5,000 US and EU consumers—outpacing industry averages of 15-20% reported by peers like Shein and ASOS. This was fueled by our "Wave of Style" multimedia campaign, a $45 million Q4 push across CTV, YouTube, and TikTok, which generated 2.1 billion impressions and a 35% increase in earned media value to $120 million. Social listening tools from Brandwatch showed a 42% YoY surge in unprompted mentions, with our hashtag #RetailWaveStyle amassing 15 million user-generated posts. Notably, video completion rates hit 78% on TikTok shoppable shorts, reflecting strong resonance in a format where Gen Z conversion funnels are compressing from awareness to purchase in under 48 hours.

Turning to customer acquisition, we added 1.45 million net new customers in Q4 alone—a 22% YoY increase and ahead of our guidance—bringing our active user base to 28 million. This translated to an 18% rise in monthly active shoppers, with acquisition cohorts showing impressive early retention: Day-30 retention for Q4 newbies at 52%, up from 45% last year. Critically, our customer acquisition cost (CAC) improved to $42, a 19% reduction from $52 in Q4 FY23, thanks to payback periods shrinking to 4.2 months versus the e-commerce benchmark of 6-8 months per Shopify's merchant data. Lifetime value (LTV) for these new customers is tracking at $285, yielding an LTV:CAC ratio of 6.8x—well above the 3x threshold for sustainable scaling.

Channel performance was the engine here. Performance marketing, which accounted for 62% of our $180 million Q4 media spend, delivered a blended ROAS of 5.2x, with Google Performance Max campaigns leading at 6.1x ROAS on a $55 million investment. We optimized for value-based bidding, prioritizing high-AOV segments like electronics (average basket $145), which saw a 14% uplift in ROAS post-implementation. Brand campaigns, at 38% of spend, punched above their weight with a 3.8x ROAS, driven by upper-funnel initiatives like our partnership with influencer collective LTK, which drove 320,000 new-to-brand customers at a blended CAC of $28.

Technically, we've supercharged this with our proprietary WaveAI personalization engine, now live across 95% of our ad stack. Using first-party data from our 1st-party CRM and server-side tracking to comply with GDPR/CCPA, it dynamically segments users into 1,200 micro-audiences based on purchase intent signals—like "abandoned cart beauty browsers" or "cross-border fashion explorers." This yielded a 31% lift in conversion rates for retargeting and a 24% reduction in frequency capping waste. We're also piloting incrementality testing via GeoLift experiments in 15 US DMAs, confirming that our TikTok For Business spend drove 27% incremental revenue—critical in an era where platforms like Meta are deprecating third-party cookies.

Regionally, performance varied but trended positively. In North America (72% of revenue), we captured 25% market share growth in fast fashion per SimilarWeb data, with CAC steady at $38 amid softening CPMs on Amazon DSP. Europe (15% of revenue) faced headwinds from higher VAT on digital ads, but our localized campaigns—tailored for Black Friday/Cyber Monday with DACH-specific creatives—boosted new customer growth 31% YoY, with ROAS at 4.7x. APAC (8% of revenue) was our star, exploding 48% in new acquisitions via Shopee and Lazada integrations, where social commerce penetration hit 65% of sales; CAC here dipped to $25, leveraging viral KOL partnerships akin to those powering Temu's blitz. Emerging markets like LATAM (5% of revenue) showed promise, with Brazil's PIX payment rails enabling 2x faster checkouts and a 40% acquisition uplift.

Strategically, these results underscore our three-pronged playbook for FY25: (1) Double down on social and shoppable commerce, allocating 40% of our $850 million annual budget to TikTok Shop and Instagram Reels, targeting a 30% ROAS floor; (2) AI-led efficiency, rolling out predictive LTV modeling to cap CAC at $40 globally, with A/B testing on 50+ creative variants weekly via our Adobe Sensei integration; (3) Omnichannel synergy, blending digital with our 150 pop-up stores, where in-store QR codes drove 15% of online acquisitions at near-zero marginal cost. Amid macroeconomic pressures—like US consumer sentiment dipping to 68 on the Conference Board index—we're insulated by our 65% gross margins on private-label SKUs, allowing aggressive reinvestment.

In summary, our marketing engine is firing on all cylinders, delivering scalable awareness and acquisition in a maturing e-commerce arena dominated by hyperscalers like Amazon and disruptors like Temu. This positions us for 20-25% top-line growth in FY25, with marketing efficiency as our competitive moat.

Next, I'd like to dive deep into our new product and service launches, which have been a key growth driver this quarter. We're thrilled with the early performance across our portfolio, reflecting strong execution on our innovation roadmap amid a competitive e-commerce landscape dominated by giants like Amazon and Shopify merchants. We've launched three major initiatives since Q3: our AI-driven RetailWave Personalize engine, the WaveGreen sustainable private-label apparel line, and RetailWave QuickShip, our same-day delivery service in urban markets. Let me break down the metrics, customer feedback, regional nuances, and strategic takeaways.

First, RetailWave Personalize, our proprietary AI recommendation engine powered by machine learning models trained on over 500 million anonymized user interactions. Rolled out to 60% of our 28 million MAUs in October, it leverages collaborative filtering and real-time behavioral data to deliver hyper-personalized product feeds, similar to how Stitch Fix uses data science but scaled for mass-market retail. Early results are outstanding: Personalize has boosted conversion rates by 28% on affected sessions, driving a 15% uplift in AOV to $78 from $68 baseline. GMV contribution from personalized carts hit $450 million in Q4, representing 12% of total GMV—ahead of our internal target of 8%. Repeat purchase rates for users exposed to Personalize jumped 22% YoY, with ARPU climbing 18% to $142.

Customer feedback has been glowing. Our post-purchase NPS for Personalize users stands at 74, versus a platform average of 62—on par with top performers like Warby Parker. App Store ratings for the updated mobile app spiked to 4.7 stars, with 85% of reviews citing 'spot-on recommendations' as a highlight. Qualitative insights from 50,000 survey responses show 62% of users discovering 3+ new products they wouldn't have found otherwise, fueling organic cross-sell into high-margin categories like electronics and beauty.

Regionally, U.S. adoption leads at 35% GMV lift, thanks to our AWS-hosted inference pipelines ensuring sub-50ms latency. In Europe, GDPR-compliant data handling has tempered growth to 20% but with superior LTV gains—European users show 25% lower churn at 4.2% monthly. APAC, particularly India and Southeast Asia via our Flipkart partnership, is at 18% uplift but scaling fast with vernacular NLP enhancements.

Strategically, this positions us ahead of Shopify's basic recs and Amazon's algorithmic black box by emphasizing transparency—users can toggle 'why this rec?' explanations, building trust in an era of privacy scrutiny post-Apple's ATT changes.

Moving to WaveGreen, our private-label sustainable apparel line launched in November across 5,000 SKUs—think organic cotton basics and recycled polyester activewear, sourced via blockchain-tracked supply chains from suppliers in Bangladesh and Vietnam. Priced 10-15% below competitors like Everlane, it taps into the $15 billion U.S. sustainable fashion market growing at 12% CAGR per McKinsey. Early traction: $120 million GMV in just six weeks, 8% of apparel category sales, with 40% attach rate to non-apparel carts via bundling algorithms. Inventory turnover is 4.2x, beating our 3.5x target, thanks to demand forecasting refined by our new Prophet time-series models.

Feedback is robust: 92% repurchase intent from 200,000 early buyers, with NPS at 68. Trustpilot reviews average 4.6 stars, praising 'affordable eco without greenwashing'—75% cite third-party certifications like GOTS as a differentiator. Social sentiment analysis via Brandwatch shows +35% buzz versus legacy lines, amplified by TikTok Shop integrations driving 25% of sales.

Regionally, North America accounts for 65% of sales (45% GMV growth), fueled by Gen Z preferences—55% of buyers under 30. EU uptake is 22% of regional GMV, boosted by EU Green Deal alignment, while APAC lags at 13% due to pricing sensitivity but shows 30% MoM growth in premium urban segments like Mumbai and Jakarta.

This launch de-risks margin pressure from third-party sellers (now 55% of GMV) by hitting 45% gross margins on WaveGreen versus 32% platform average, directly countering Temu's ultra-low pricing wars.

Finally, RetailWave QuickShip, our quick-commerce service partnering with DoorDash and Gopuff for same-day delivery in 25 U.S. metros and London, Berlin pilots. Targeting the $50 billion U.S. quick-commerce boom (per eMarketer), it guarantees 2-hour delivery on 80% of 1P inventory. Beta GMV: $280 million, 7% of total, with 35% order volume growth WoW. Fulfillment costs are controlled at 18% of GMV via dynamic routing ML, keeping take rates steady at 22%.

Customer love is evident: 82% satisfaction rate, NPS 72, with 4.8-star ratings emphasizing speed. Churn among QuickShip users is half the platform average at 2.1%, extending LTV by 30% to $210. Feedback highlights frictionless tracking—68% via AR-enabled app previews.

U.S. dominates at 85% penetration, with NYC and LA at 50%+ repeat rates. EU pilots show 25% GMV share but higher CAC at $18 versus U.S. $12, offset by 40% AOV premium. APAC expansion queued for Q1 Singapore.

Strategic insights and outlook: These launches contributed 22% to Q4's 25% YoY revenue growth to $2.1 billion, with blended NPS uplift of 9 points. Technically, we're investing $150 million in 2025 for edge computing to cut latency 40%, enabling social commerce tie-ins like Instagram Checkout. Competitively, we're carving niche vs. Amazon's scale via agility—CAC payback now 4 months on new services. Risks include supply chain volatility (mitigated by 20% buffer stock) and macroeconomic headwinds curbing discretionary spend. Looking ahead, we expect these to drive 25%+ GMV acceleration in Q1 FY25, with full Personalize rollout and WaveGreen expansion to home goods.

As we unpack another key driver behind our results this quarter, let's turn to the impact of our promotional activities on both top-line sales and bottom-line profitability. In the hyper-competitive E-Commerce landscape—where players like Amazon, Alibaba, and Shein are constantly battling for share of wallet—promotions remain a double-edged sword. They turbocharge Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) and customer acquisition but can erode margins if not executed with precision. I'll break this down with specifics from our playbook, including quantitative impacts, regional nuances, technical enablers, and our strategic evolution.

Sales acceleration: A 28% GMV uplift quarter-over-quarter. Our promotional cadence in Q4 delivered a robust 28% QoQ lift in GMV, pushing total GMV to $5.0 billion, up 22% YoY. This was fueled by a multi-pronged strategy blending evergreen discounts, flash sales, and event-driven campaigns. For context, our core promotional levers included sitewide discounts and bundle offers: We rolled out 20-30% off on high-velocity categories like apparel (think fast-fashion SKUs akin to Shein's model) and consumer electronics, which accounted for 45% of promo-driven GMV. This drove a 35% increase in order volume to 22 million orders, with Average Order Value (AOV) holding steady at $227—thanks to cross-sell bundles like "Buy a laptop, get 25% off accessories," which boosted basket size by 12%.

Flash sales and limited-time deals: Mirroring Amazon Prime Day dynamics, our "Global Flash Fest" (a 48-hour event in mid-December) generated $850 million in incremental GMV, a 40% YoY jump. Conversion rates spiked 22% during these windows, from our baseline 3.2% to nearly 4.0%, as push notifications via our mobile app reached 65 million active users.

Loyalty-tiered promos: For our Wave Elite subscribers (28 million members, up 18% YoY), we offered exclusive 15% cashback on groceries and beauty—categories resilient amid inflation. This segment alone contributed 55% of promo sales, with repeat purchase rates climbing to 42% within 30 days.

Trend-wise, we've seen promotions shift from broad blasts to hyper-targeted execution. Post-iOS privacy changes (ATT), our reliance on first-party data has grown, enabling 2x better uplift from personalized promos versus generic ones. Compared to peers, our promo-driven GMV growth outpaced Shopify merchants' average 12% quarterly bump and aligned with Zalando's Euro-focused flash sale performance.

Profitability trade-offs: Gross margin compression offset by scale. Promotions compressed our adjusted gross margin by 420 basis points QoQ to 42%, down from 46.2% in Q3. This reflects a promo cost of sales at 8.5% of GMV (up from 6.2% last year), driven by deeper discounts and higher fulfillment costs during peak traffic. Key margin drags included a promo discount rate of 22.1% (up 3.6 points YoY due to deeper cuts in apparel to counter Shein/Temu pricing wars), fulfillment as 12.3% of GMV (up 50 bps from surge volume straining our 150 FC network and last-mile costs up 7% due to fuel inflation), returns rate on promo orders at 18% (up 3 points from impulse buys in fashion), and contribution margin post-promo at 22.4% (down 270 bps but fixed costs amortized better at scale).

Despite this, we delivered positive operating leverage, with adjusted EBITDA margins expanding 150 bps YoY to 12.5% on $5.0B GMV. Why? Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) on promo marketing hit 4.8x, versus industry benchmarks of 3-4x for Walmart or Target e-comm. Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) for promo-acquired users was $18, 20% below non-promo cohorts, thanks to efficient channels like Google Shopping and TikTok Shop integrations.

Regional breakdown: Tailored plays in a fragmented market. North America (52% of GMV): Black Friday preview events and holiday tie-ins drove 32% sales lift, but margins dipped 500 bps due to aggressive Amazon matching. Hero products like Apple AirPods bundles flew off shelves, with AOV up 8% to $245.

Europe (28% of GMV): GDPR-compliant personalization yielded 25% uplift, led by holiday sales in fashion (à la ASOS). UK and Germany saw 15% YoY GMV growth despite economic headwinds, but returns hit 20% from sizing issues.

APAC (15% of GMV): Year-end warm-ups in China (via our Tmall partnership) exploded with 55% QoQ growth, fueled by live-streaming promos on Douyin. India’s festive deals via Flipkart alliance boosted volume 40%, though low AOV ($45) pressured margins to 32%.

Rest of World (5%): Emerging markets like LATAM saw 22% growth from wallet-financing promos (e.g., Mercado Pago integrations), but forex volatility added 2% margin drag.

Technical initiatives: Data-driven promo optimization. Our AI-powered dynamic pricing engine—built on AWS SageMaker and proprietary RL models—adjusts discounts in real-time based on demand elasticity, inventory levels, and competitor pricing (scraped via Bright Data). This reduced "over-discounting" by 15%, saving $45 million in Q4.

Other enablers: Personalization at scale using Snowflake for customer 360 views, serving 1.2 billion tailored promo emails/SMS, lifting open rates to 28% and click-through to 12%. Omnichannel sync: Buy-online-pickup-in-store (BOPIS) promos during peaks cut fulfillment costs 10% by leveraging our 2,000 micro-fulfillment centers. Fraud mitigation: ML models flagged 3% of promo traffic as bots, protecting $120 million in GMV.

Strategic insights: Evolving beyond discounts. Promotions drove 60% of new customer acquisition this quarter, but Lifetime Value (LTV) for promo cohorts is now tracking at 3.2x CAC over 12 months—up from 2.5x last year—via post-promo upsell funnels. Key shifts: (1) Subscription pivot: Expanding Wave Elite with zero-fee returns and 10% perpetual discounts, targeting 35 million members by FYE. This mirrors Amazon Prime's success, with early cohorts showing 40% higher LTV. (2) Value-based pricing: Less % off, more "free gift with purchase" on private-label brands (e.g., our WaveEssentials line, 25% margins). (3) Sustainability angle: "Green promos" (eco-packaging discounts) resonated in EU, boosting brand loyalty 15%. (4) GenAI experiments: Testing chat-based haggling to personalize deals, with pilot ROAS at 6x.

In summary, Q4 promos were a sales powerhouse—$1.1 billion incremental GMV—but disciplined execution preserved EBITDA at $625 million. For FY25, we guide to 20-25% GMV growth with gross margins stabilizing at 41-42%, leaning into targeted, tech-fueled campaigns amid holiday ramps.

Finally, on our take rate, which came in at 14.2% of GMV this quarter—up 40 basis points year-over-year from 13.8% and 20 basis points sequentially from Q3's 14.0%. This marks our sixth straight quarter of take rate expansion, driving $710 million in marketplace revenue on $5.0 billion of GMV, a 25% YoY increase. For context, this outperforms peers like Shopify, which reported a blended payments and services take rate around 2.8% on GPV, and positions us closer to Amazon's marketplace segment at roughly 15% on third-party sales. Let me break down the key changes and drivers behind this improvement, with a focus on pricing, promotions, mix shifts, technical initiatives, and regional dynamics.

First, pricing discipline was the largest contributor, accounting for about 25 basis points of expansion. In October, we rolled out a refined tiered fee structure for our Pro Sellers—our top 20% of merchants by volume, who represent 65% of GMV. High-volume sellers in categories like electronics and fashion now pay a base fulfillment fee of 11.5% plus 2% FBA-style logistics, down from a flat 14% for everyone pre-adjustment. Conversely, we introduced a 16.5% premium fee tier for low-volume or high-touch categories like luxury goods and perishables, capturing more value from ASPs above $150. This shift mirrors Etsy’s category-specific pricing but with more granularity, boosting overall take rate by optimizing for seller elasticity—we saw a 3% uptick in Pro Seller retention post-change, with no material GMV migration to off-platform channels.

Promotions drove another 15 basis points, but strategically contained to high-ROI cohorts. We ran targeted fee waivers—fully absorbing the 2.5% transaction fee for the first $10,000 in GMV—for 50,000 new SMB sellers in our RetailWave Accelerate program, focused on underrepresented categories like home & garden and beauty. This generated $450 million in incremental GMV from these sellers, with a payback period under 18 months as they graduate to full fees. We also layered in co-op promotions with brands like Procter & Gamble and Unilever, where we subsidized 1% of ad fees in exchange for exclusive Prime-eligible listings, lifting attach rates for our sponsored products from 18% to 21% of GMV. Importantly, these were 30% more efficient than last year's broad-based holiday waivers, which had diluted take rate by 10 basis points in Q4 2023.

Shifting to mix effects, which added 10 basis points, we benefited from a favorable product and seller composition. Electronics and consumer packaged goods (CPG), our highest-margin segments at 16-18% take rates, grew to 42% of GMV from 38% YoY, driven by AI-recommended bundling—think Apple AirPods paired with Belkin chargers. Conversely, low-take commoditized categories like groceries stabilized at 12% of GMV after our exit from unprofitable third-party fresh fulfillment partnerships. Seller mix tilted toward enterprise brands (e.g., integrations with Shopify Plus merchants migrating 15% more volume to RetailWave), which pay higher ad and data fees, contributing 3% to take rate via our 28% ASP-matched advertising yield.

On the technical front, our investments in machine learning have been game-changers, indirectly supporting 20 basis points of expansion through reduced leakage. Our Dynamic Take Optimizer—launched in beta last year and now covering 70% of transactions—uses real-time RL models to adjust fees microsecond-by-microsecond based on buyer intent, cart abandonment risk, and competitive pricing from Sea Limited's Shopee or PDD Holdings' Temu. This lifted conversion by 4.2%, minimizing refund rates from 2.1% to 1.8% and clawbacks that erode effective take. Additionally, blockchain-verified supply chain pilots with 500 suppliers reduced fraud-related chargebacks by 25%, preserving $50 million in revenue. These initiatives align with industry trends, like Amazon's Rufus AI shopping assistant, but with a sharper focus on fee recapture.

Regionally, the story varies but remains positive. In North America, our core market at 55% of GMV, take rate hit 15.4%—up 60 bps YoY—fueled by Wave Elite loyalty (85% of US orders) and denser logistics networks yielding 3% lower fulfillment costs passed back as seller incentives. Europe saw 13.9%, a 30 bps gain despite VAT headwinds and competition from Zalando, thanks to localized pricing in GBP and EUR tiers. APAC, now 25% of GMV after our Lazada stake acquisition, expanded from 11.2% to 12.1%, driven by aggressive promotions in Indonesia and India to counter Temu's ultra-low pricing—though we expect normalization as our 0-1 click checkout rolls out there next quarter. Emerging markets like LATAM lagged at 10.8% due to higher promo intensity amid inflation, but pilots with Mercado Libre integrations are bridging the gap.

Strategically, these dynamics underscore our "Value Density" thesis: prioritizing high-ASP, high-frequency categories while using data flywheels to outpace discounters. Amid macroeconomic pressures—U.S. consumer trading down 7% in basket value per Nielsen data—our take rate resilience reflects sticky ecosystem economics, with 92% seller NPS and cross-sell into ads/services at 35% adoption.

Looking ahead, we guide to 14.4-14.6% take rate in Q1 FY25, with 30-40 bps expansion in FY25, assuming stable FX and no major tariff escalations from U.S.-China trade tensions. Key levers include full Dynamic Take rollout, new premium tiers for GenAI-generated listings, and APAC logistics scale. We're confident this compounds our marketplace moat, targeting 16%+ by 2027.

Operator, we are now ready for questions.

Operator:
Instructions for the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Mike Chen with Goldman Sachs.

Mike Chen:
Thanks for taking my question. Jordan, your marketing metrics look impressive with CAC down and ROAS up, but with ad platforms tightening privacy, how sustainable is this LTV:CAC ratio heading into FY25, especially in APAC where you're scaling aggressively?

Alex Rivera:
Thanks, Mike. Great question. Sustainability comes from our WaveAI engine and first-party data focus, which we've proven with 27% incremental lift from GeoLift tests. In APAC, KOL partnerships keep CAC low at $25, and we're targeting that 6.8x ratio firm through predictive LTV models. Taylor can add on ops side if needed, but we're confident.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Patel with Morgan Stanley.

Lisa Patel:
Hi, team. On the new launches, Personalize and QuickShip are driving nice GMV, but scaling to full rollout—any risks to margins or fulfillment capacity, particularly with WaveGreen's inventory turnover?

Jordan Lee:
Hi Lisa, thanks. Margins are protected—WaveGreen at 45% gross, QuickShip fulfillment at 18% of GMV via ML routing. Capacity: We're adding edge computing and 20% buffer stock, with Prophet models keeping turnover above 4x. Early LTV gains from low churn cohorts more than offset, positioning us for 25% acceleration.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Wong with JPMorgan.

David Wong:
Thanks. Jordan, promos juiced sales but compressed margins 420 bps—how are you balancing H2 aggression with profitability, and does take rate expansion help offset in high-promo regions like APAC?

Taylor Kim:
David, thanks. From ops, we're shifting to value-based like free gifts and Elite subs, which lifted LTV 3.2x CAC. Take rate gains—12.1% in APAC via tiered pricing—directly offset promo intensity, with Dynamic Optimizer recapturing fees. Jordan's guidance has margins stabilizing at 41-42%, and we're lean on BOPIS to cut costs.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn the call back over to Alex Rivera for closing remarks.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for joining us today. We are confident in our ability to continue to execute our strategy and deliver long-term value for our shareholders. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
